title: Church History: Reformation to Today
summary: From Luther's Ninety-five Theses to the global church of today: the Reformation, revivals, the modern missionary movement, and the shift of Christianity to the global South.
description: This course follows the church from 1517 to the present: the Protestant Reformation and its leaders, the Catholic response, the Puritans and Pietists, the Great Awakenings and the Wesleys, the modern missionary movement that brought the gospel to Nigeria, the challenges of liberal theology, the rise of Pentecostalism and evangelicalism, and the growth of the church in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
objectives: Explain the causes, leaders and teachings of the Reformation
Describe the different branches of the Reformation and the Catholic response
Trace the revivals of the 17th and 18th centuries
Describe the main developments of the 20th and 21st centuries
outcomes: Explain the significance of 1517 and the five solas
Distinguish Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist and Anglican reform
Describe the ministries of Wesley, Whitefield and Edwards
Explain William Carey's role in modern missions
Explain the growth of the church in the global South

modules.title: The Protestant Reformation
modules.intro: In the sixteenth century the church was reformed by a return to Scripture. This week we study Luther, Zwingli, Calvin and the Anabaptists.

lessons.title: Luther and the Ninety-five Theses
lessons.body:
Martin Luther, a German monk and professor, was troubled by the sale of indulgences. On **31 October 1517** he posted **Ninety-five Theses** for debate in Wittenberg. Printed copies spread rapidly.

Studying Romans, Luther came to see that "The just shall live by faith" (Romans 1:17): righteousness is God's gift received by faith, not earned.

At the **Diet of Worms** (1521), ordered to recant his writings, Luther refused unless convinced by Scripture or plain reason, saying his conscience was captive to the Word of God. He then translated the New Testament into German so ordinary people could read it.

lessons.title: Zwingli, Calvin and the Reformed churches
lessons.body:
In Zurich, **Ulrich Zwingli** began preaching through Matthew verse by verse in 1519 and reformed worship according to Scripture.

**John Calvin**, a Frenchman, led reform in Geneva. His *Institutes of the Christian Religion* (first edition 1536) became the most influential Protestant theology, stressing God's sovereignty, Scripture and grace. Geneva trained pastors who spread Reformed churches to France, the Netherlands and Scotland, where **John Knox** led the reform.

The reformers' teaching is often summarised in the **five solas**: Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, and the glory of God alone.

lessons.title: Anabaptists, England and the Catholic response
lessons.body:
**Anabaptists** ('re-baptizers'), beginning in Zurich in 1525, believed only professing believers should be baptized and that the church should be separate from the state. They were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. Mennonites descend from them, and Baptists share some of their convictions.

In **England**, Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 for political reasons, but true reform came through William Tyndale's English New Testament and leaders like Thomas Cranmer. The **King James Version** followed in 1611.

The **Catholic Church** responded at the **Council of Trent** (1545-1563), correcting some abuses but rejecting justification by faith alone. The Jesuits led Catholic missions worldwide.

terms.def: Luther's 1517 propositions against the sale of indulgences.
The 1521 assembly where Luther refused to recant.
Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, glory to God alone.
John Calvin's major work of Protestant theology (1536).
Radical reformers who practised believer's baptism and church-state separation.
The Catholic council (1545-1563) that responded to the Reformation.

texts.teaches: The just shall live by faith.
By grace are ye saved through faith.
Judge whether it is right to hearken to men more than to God.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God.
To God be glory for ever.

summary: Zwingli and Calvin led the Reformed churches; Knox led in Scotland.
Anabaptists practised believer's baptism and were persecuted.
England broke with Rome; Trent was the Catholic response.

questions.q: When did Luther post the Ninety-five Theses?
Who wrote the Institutes of the Christian Religion?

modules.title: Puritans, Pietists and Awakenings
modules.intro: After the Reformation came movements of deeper devotion and great revival. This week covers about 1600 to 1800.

lessons.title: Puritans and Pietists
lessons.body:
The **Puritans** in England wanted the church further 'purified' according to Scripture. They stressed preaching, holy living, the sabbath and family worship. Writers such as John Owen, Richard Baxter and **John Bunyan**, a Baptist who wrote *The Pilgrim's Progress* in prison, still bless believers. Some Puritans sailed to New England in search of religious freedom.

In Germany, **Pietism**, led by Philipp Jakob Spener and August Hermann Francke, stressed personal faith, Bible study in small groups and care for orphans. The **Moravians** under Count Zinzendorf began a prayer meeting in 1727 that continued for a hundred years and sent missionaries far and wide.

lessons.title: The Wesleys and the Evangelical Revival
lessons.body:
**John Wesley**, an Anglican priest, felt his heart "strangely warmed" at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, in 1738 as he heard Luther's preface to Romans read. With his brother **Charles**, who wrote thousands of hymns, he preached in the open air to miners and the poor.

Wesley organised converts into societies and small 'classes' for accountability. This became the **Methodist** movement, which spread worldwide, including to Nigeria.

Wesley taught Christian perfection and conditional security, and worked against slavery. His friend **George Whitefield**, a Calvinist, preached to great crowds in Britain and America. They differed on doctrine but both preached the new birth.

lessons.title: The Great Awakening
lessons.body:
In the American colonies the **First Great Awakening** (1730s-1740s) brought many to Christ. **Jonathan Edwards**, a Reformed pastor and theologian, saw revival in Northampton and carefully described marks of true and false religious experience. Whitefield's preaching tours spread the revival.

Revivals produced conversions, changed lives, new churches, and later campaigns against slavery and for education.

Revival is God's work: "Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?" (Psalm 85:6). Edwards taught that true revival is marked by love for Christ, hatred of sin, love for Scripture and love for others, not merely by emotional excitement (compare 1 John 4:1-6).

terms.def: English Protestants who sought further reform of the church according to Scripture.
A German movement stressing personal faith, Bible study and holy living.
Followers of Zinzendorf known for continuous prayer and pioneering missions.
The movement begun by John and Charles Wesley, organised in societies and classes.
The revival in the American colonies in the 1730s-1740s.
A season when God renews His people and many are converted.

texts.teaches: Ye must be born again.
The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost.
Wilt thou not revive us again?
O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years.
Try the spirits whether they are of God.

summary: Puritans pursued Scripture-based reform and holy living.
Pietists and Moravians stressed personal faith, prayer and mission.
The Wesleys and Whitefield led the Evangelical Revival.
Edwards described the marks of true revival.

questions.q: Where was John Wesley's heart 'strangely warmed'?
Which movement did the Wesleys begin?
Who described the marks of true revival?

modules.title: The Great Century of Missions
modules.intro: The nineteenth century saw the gospel carried worldwide. This week covers the missionary movement, including its arrival in West Africa.

lessons.title: William Carey and modern missions
lessons.body:
**William Carey**, an English Baptist shoemaker, wrote *An Enquiry* (1792) arguing that the Great Commission still applies. He preached "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God" and helped form the Baptist Missionary Society.

In 1793 Carey sailed to India, where he worked for over forty years, translating Scripture into many languages and opposing widow-burning.

Mission societies multiplied: the London Missionary Society (1795), the Church Missionary Society (1799), American boards and many more. The nineteenth century is often called the 'great century' of missions.

lessons.title: Missions to Africa and Nigeria
lessons.body:
Freed slaves resettled in Sierra Leone became Christians, and some returned to their homelands, including Yorubaland, asking for missionaries.

In **1842** the Methodist **Thomas Birch Freeman** reached Badagry, followed by Henry Townsend of the Church Missionary Society. **Samuel Ajayi Crowther**, a Yoruba man rescued from a slave ship, was ordained and in **1864** became the first African Anglican bishop. He led the translation of the Bible into Yoruba.

Presbyterians arrived in Calabar in 1846; **Mary Slessor** later worked there for decades and opposed the killing of twins. American Southern Baptists began work in 1850 through Thomas Jefferson Bowen, and the Sudan Interior Mission entered the north in the 1890s.

lessons.title: Strengths and failures of the missionary era
lessons.body:
Missionaries brought the gospel, Bible translation in mother tongues, schools and hospitals. Many died of disease; parts of West Africa were called 'the white man's grave'. African evangelists, catechists and translators did much of the work.

There were also failures: some missionaries shared colonial attitudes, treated African culture as wholly evil, or kept Africans out of leadership. Crowther himself faced racial opposition late in life.

These failures led many Africans to start independent churches, and they remind us that the gospel belongs to every culture. The lesson: honour faithful pioneers, repent of prejudice, and pursue partnership.

terms.def: The worldwide spread of Protestant missions from the 1790s.
English Baptist missionary to India (1793) often called the father of modern missions.
Anglican mission society founded in 1799, active in Nigeria from 1842.
Yoruba bishop (1864), the first African Anglican bishop, Bible translator.
Scottish missionary in Calabar who opposed the killing of twins.
Coastal town where Christian missions in Nigeria began in 1842.

texts.teaches: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them.
Enlarge the place of thy tent.
How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel.
Come over and help us.
I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.

summary: William Carey sparked the modern missionary movement in 1792-1793.
Missions reached Badagry in 1842; Crowther became bishop in 1864.
Missionaries brought Scripture, schools and hospitals at great cost.
Colonial attitudes also caused harm and led to African independent churches.

questions.q: Where did Christian missions in Nigeria begin in 1842?
Who became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864?

modules.title: The Twentieth Century and the Global Church
modules.intro: The last century brought new challenges and astonishing growth. This week we study liberalism, evangelicalism, Pentecostalism and the global South.

lessons.title: Liberalism and evangelical response
lessons.body:
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries **liberal theology** questioned the Bible's inspiration, miracles, the virgin birth and the bodily resurrection, reducing Christianity to moral teaching.

Believers responded. Some, called **fundamentalists**, defended 'the fundamentals' of the faith. Later **evangelicals**, such as Billy Graham, John Stott and Carl Henry, combined faithfulness to Scripture with engagement in society. The **Lausanne Congress** (1974) gathered evangelicals worldwide to commit to world evangelisation.

Paul's warning remains: "preach the word... For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine" (2 Timothy 4:2-3).

lessons.title: Pentecostal and charismatic growth
lessons.body:
In 1906 a revival at **Azusa Street** in Los Angeles, led by **William Seymour**, an African American preacher, spread Pentecostalism worldwide. Its emphasis on the baptism in the Spirit, tongues and healing found fertile soil in Africa, Latin America and Asia.

From the 1960s the **charismatic renewal** brought similar experiences into older churches. In Africa, the Aladura churches, the 1930 revival under Joseph Babalola, and campus revivals of the 1970s produced vibrant Pentecostal churches.

Pentecostals and charismatics are now among the largest groups of Christians in the world. (A later course studies these movements in detail.)

lessons.title: The shift to the global South
lessons.body:
In 1900 most Christians lived in Europe and North America. Today most live in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Africa has seen remarkable church growth over the past century, and Nigeria has one of the largest Christian populations in the world.

This brings opportunity and responsibility: African churches now send missionaries, write theology and lead global bodies. It also brings challenges: shallow discipleship, prosperity teaching, syncretism, division, and persecution.

The church's history shows God's faithfulness: "I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18). Our generation must hand on the faith faithfully (2 Timothy 2:2).

terms.def: Theology that doubts the Bible's inspiration and miracles, stressing moral teaching.
A movement defending the fundamental doctrines of the faith against liberalism.
A movement stressing Scripture, the cross, conversion and active witness.
The 1974 world gathering of evangelicals for world evangelisation.
The 1906 revival in Los Angeles that spread Pentecostalism worldwide.
Africa, Asia and Latin America, where most Christians now live.

texts.teaches: The time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine.
If Christ is not raised, your faith is vain.
God will pour out His Spirit upon all flesh.
A great multitude of all nations stands before the throne.
Commit the faith to faithful men who shall teach others.

summary: Liberal theology denied core truths; evangelicals defended them.
Most Christians now live in the global South, including Nigeria.
Growth brings both opportunity and the duty of faithful discipleship.

assignments.title: The Reformation today
assignments.prompt: Explain the main teachings recovered at the Reformation. Then show, with examples, why each is still needed in churches in Nigeria today. Use at least four Bible passages.

assignments.title: A missionary biography
assignments.prompt: Write a short biography of one person from this course (for example Samuel Ajayi Crowther, Mary Slessor, William Carey or John Wesley). Describe their life, their contribution, their struggles and the lessons for believers today.
